lineages.name: João Gilberto
lineages.why: Invented the batida and the near-spoken vocal delivery; his 1958 single 'Chega de Saudade' and the 1959 LP are taken as the birth of bossa nova. He was an obsessive perfectionist — 28 takes of 'Rosa Morena' to get one vowel right — and recorded voice and guitar on separate mics at equal level.

lineages.name: Antônio Carlos Jobim
lineages.why: The genre's main composer: a pianist who studied with Koellreutter and took harmony from Debussy and Ravel, writing melodies that dwell on major sevenths over sophisticated substitutions. With Vinicius de Moraes from 1956; later arranged with Claus Ogerman (Wave, 1967).

lineages.name: Milton Banana
lineages.why: Drummer on Chega de Saudade and Getz/Gilberto who set the bossa nova kit style: quiet, flexible, dynamic, fitted to Gilberto's guitar rather than to a fixed bass-drum ostinato. He recalled that Gilberto's thoroughness made sessions long.

lineages.name: Stan Getz and Creed Taylor
lineages.why: Jazz Samba (with Charlie Byrd, 1962) and Getz/Gilberto (produced by Taylor, recorded 1963, released 1964) took the style to the US charts; Getz/Gilberto was the first non-American album to win Album of the Year.

name: Bossa nova

notes.text: The batida is a reduction of samba batucada: the thumb stylizes the surdo, the index, middle and ring fingers phrase like a tamborim. The feel keeps samba's emphasis on beat 2 of a 2/4 bar.

The finger pattern is a two-bar cycle, usually taught in 4/4 cut time; João Gilberto's recordings use many variants — a study of two of his 1960 tracks found 19 patterns or variations, organized in pairs of bars, some anticipating the odd bar and some the even.

The bass (the guitarist's thumb, or an upright doubling it) alternates root and fifth on beats 1 and 3, with an occasional bounce on the upbeat before the next beat; chord changes are anticipated on the 'and' of the previous beat rather than struck on the downbeat.

Chord colour is the idiom: maj9, 6/9, 11ths, 13ths, b9s and 7#5, voiced in four (sometimes five) parts. Jobim favours ii-bII7-I (tritone substitution) and II7#11 over plain ii-V-I, and bridges that modulate without ever stating the new tonic.
Jobim drew on Debussy and Ravel as well as Pixinguinha and Ary Barroso; his melodies often insist on the major seventh of the chord rather than resolving to the root.
Standards are song forms: Girl from Ipanema is 40 bars, AABA, with a 16-bar bridge made of four four-bar phrases, three of them sequences of the first.

The singing is quiet, near-conversational and unornamented — João Gilberto recorded voice and guitar on separate microphones so they sat at equal level — a break from the operatic style that came before.

Drums are understated: Milton Banana, on Chega de Saudade and Getz/Gilberto, played with subtlety and dynamics rather than a fixed set of licks — Jazz Samba needed two American drummers to approximate what he did alone.

The export sound adds a jazz soloist and strings to the guitar and voice: Getz's tenor on Getz/Gilberto (Jobim on piano, Milton Banana on drums and pandeiro), Claus Ogerman's strings on Jobim's Wave (1967).

Getz/Gilberto was recorded in two days (18–19 March 1963) at A & R Recording, engineered by Phil Ramone, and won the 1965 Grammy for Best Engineered Recording: an intimate, uncompressed acoustic balance is the reference.

Lyrics are conversational and self-aware: Newton Mendonça's 'Desafinado' answers critics who said bossa nova was for singers without voices by turning it into a love song about being 'off-key'. Vinicius de Moraes was Jobim's main lyricist.

Born in the Copacabana clubs of Beco das Garrafas in the late 1950s; the canonical instrument is the nylon-string guitar, with piano, upright bass, brushes and a tenor sax or flute in the jazz versions.

pitfalls.text: Playing it as swing or as a set of drum licks. The feel is samba-derived and straight, and the drummer follows the guitar's batida with dynamics rather than a fixed pattern.
Changing chords squarely on the downbeat and filling every gap. Anticipate changes on the preceding 'and', and keep embellishments sparse so the texture stays open when others play.
Singing out with vibrato and ornament. The idiom is near-speech volume, unornamented, with the voice balanced level with the guitar.
Resolving every ii-V the textbook way. Use tritone substitutes, dominant IIs and backdoor dominants, and let bridges modulate without cadencing.

progressions.text: Girl from Ipanema's A section: a dominant II borrowed for colour, then a ii-bII7-I tritone-substitute cadence home.
One Note Samba's twist on iii-VI-ii-V: tritone substitutes turn the roots into a descending chromatic line.
The Ipanema bridge moves: IV to bVII in successive keys, never resolving to their I.
Manhã de Carnaval is built of minor ii-Vs in A minor alternating with major ii-Vs in the relative C major.

evidence.inferred: Median and span of the tempos songbpm.com reports (in 4/4 cut-time quarters) for five reference recordings: Girl from Ipanema 132, Chega de Saudade 136, Corcovado 140, Getz's Desafinado 144, João Gilberto's Desafinado 164 (pages https://songbpm.com/@antonio-carlos-jobim/girl-from-ipanema, /@joao-gilberto/chega-de-saudade, /@antonio-carlos-jobim/corcovado, /@stan-getz/desafinado, /@joao-gilberto/desafinado).
The cited João Gilberto transcription study finds the thumb basses fall on the beginnings of the beats with only occasional anticipations, and the Acoustic Guitar lesson puts them on 1 and 3.
Girl from Ipanema's A section (Fmaj7, G7#11, Gm7, Gb7#11, Fmaj7 over eight bars, per Learn Jazz Standards) is about 0.6 a bar; the chord-a-bar sequences of One Note Samba set the upper end.

In the cited Girl from Ipanema A section two of four chords (the II7 and the bII7 tritone substitute) are outside the key, and the cited bridge never touches its keys' tonics; Jobim's borrowed and substitute dominants keep the ratio well under pop's.
Four distinct chords in the cited Girl from Ipanema A section, plus a bridge that passes through three key centres; the upper bound counts a full 40-bar AABA chorus.
João Gilberto's Desafinado runs 1:57 and Chega de Saudade 3:26 (songbpm.com); the Getz/Gilberto tracks run 2:47 to 5:27 (Wikipedia).

references.listenFor: Throughout: the guitar's thumb keeps the bass on the main beats while the fingers' syncopated chords and the quiet voice move around it.

summary: A quiet, relaxed samba from late-1950s Rio: João Gilberto reduced the samba batucada to one nylon-string guitar, the thumb standing in for the surdo and the fingers for the tamborim, under near-spoken singing. Jobim's harmony — major sevenths, ninths, #11s, tritone substitutions and unresolved modulations — sits on that steady syncopated batida.
